verdict.rationale: cubic's custom agents are documented review rules that enforce an organization's own best practices. They are configurable via cubic.yaml. Linked guidance (AGENTS.md, .cursorrules, context files, Confluence and Notion docs) feeds into reviews, and community discussion confirms the plain-English rule approach. AST or structural pattern rules are not evidenced, and enforcement relies on semantic interpretation rather than deterministic checks. missing for 10: AST/structural pattern rules, documentation of rule syntax and enforcement semantics (e.g., blocking vs commenting), independent hands-on corroboration that custom rules are reliably enforced

support.subject: As an engineering lead, I encode my team's own review guidelines — natural-language rules, AST patterns, or linked style guides — and the reviewer enforces them

citations.quote: Custom agents are review rules that enforce your organization's specific best practices across pull requests.
Custom agents: Enforce your team's coding standards
`cubic.yaml` lives in the root of your repository and becomes the source of truth for AI review behavior, ignore patterns, PR descriptions, and custom agents.
cubic automatically detects and uses context files in your repository, including `README.md`, `context.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `.cursorrules`, agent skills directories, and files in `.ai/` directories.
Pull documentation from Confluence to provide the AI with better context for code reviews, helping it understand your architecture decisions
